summary:
Charter's "Steal this idea" column profiles how Wiley, a 5,000-person publishing company, is expanding access to personalized coaching without a large budget by building an internal, homegrown pool of coaches.

Context: Charter previously covered LinkedIn's "coaching for all" benefit, which extended access to a human coach to all 17,500 LinkedIn employees. The question the piece raises is what employers can do if they want similar breadth of coaching access but lack LinkedIn-scale budget.

Wiley's approach is layered. Like many employers, it pays for external professional coaches for some senior or high-level employees. It has also added an AI coaching platform through an external vendor, AceUp. On top of those two paid layers, it is developing its own internal "coaching army" of employee coaches who can be deployed across the organization, which addresses the cost problem cited by David Smolski, Wiley's director of learning and development, who notes that sending people to professional coaches is expensive.

The framing is a talent development and L and D cost-efficiency play: internal coaching capacity as a scalable alternative to per-seat external coaching spend, with AI coaching tools filling a middle tier. The excerpt is brief and does not detail selection, training, certification, matching, or measurement of the internal coach program, nor does it give cost comparisons or outcome data.

No workplace-experience, facilities, visitor management, desk or room booking, attendance, or hybrid policy content appears in this item. It is a people and learning development story rather than a workplace-technology or space-operations story.

Sending employees to external professional coaches is costly
